extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of mathematical logic (undergraduate/graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, construction methods, and metatheorems for propositional and first-order logic: completeness, Lindenbaum's extension, compactness, syntax (wffs, sentences, substitution), semantics (structures, satisfaction), and related proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete set (Definition 42A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set Γ of sentences is complete iff for any sentence α, either α ∈ Γ or ¬α ∈ Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete sets ‘leave no questions unanswered’: for every sentence the set contains either it or its negation. Completeness of a theory has semantic/decidability consequences (e.g., a complete axiomatizable theory is decidable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure under connectives for complete consistent sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For a complete consistent set Γ: it contains α ∧ β iff it contains both α and β; it contains α ∨ β iff it contains at least one of α or β; ¬α ∈ Γ iff α ∉ Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties are crucial for constructing valuations and proving the Truth Lemma; they follow from completeness and consistency and are used to reduce satisfaction of complex formulas to membership conditions in Γ.

rubrics_metrics.name: If Γ is complete and consistent then Γ ⊢ α implies α ∈ Γ (Proposition 42B(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose Γ is complete and consistent. If Γ ⊢ α, then α ∈ Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if α ∉ Γ then completeness gives ¬α ∈ Γ and Proposition 35C yields inconsistency. This fact is used in equivalences relating semantic entailment and syntactic derivability inside complete consistent sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication membership criterion in complete sets (Proposition 42B(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: For complete consistent Γ: α → β ∈ Γ iff either α ∉ Γ or β ∈ Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward direction: if α→β ∈ Γ but α ∈ Γ and β ∉ Γ one derives a contradiction. Reverse direction uses completeness to derive α→β when α ∉ Γ (so ¬α ∈ Γ) or when β ∈ Γ. This equivalence is used in the inductive Truth Lemma step for implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lindenbaum's Lemma (Lemma 43A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every consistent set Γ in a language L can be extended to a set Γ* that is both consistent and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: enumerate all sentences α0, α1, …; set Γ0 = Γ; for each n, let Γn+1 = Γn ∪ {αn} if that is consistent, otherwise Γn ∪ {¬αn}; finally Γ* = ⋃n Γn. Prove each Γn is consistent and that finite subsets of Γ* are contained in some Γn, hence consistent; completeness follows since every sentence or its negation is added at some stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit construction method for Γ* (enumeration/extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an enumeration of all sentences, extend Γ stepwise by at each stage adding either αn if Γn ∪ {αn} is consistent, otherwise adding ¬αn; take the union as Γ*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key checks: (i) show by induction each Γn is consistent, (ii) show unions preserve consistency because every finite subset lies in some Γn, and (iii) show completeness since each sentence appears in the enumeration and either it or its negation was added when processed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation determined by a complete consistent set (Definition 44A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a complete consistent set Γ*, define valuation v(Γ*)(p) = T iff propositional atom p ∈ Γ*; otherwise v(Γ*)(p) = F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines truth-values of atomic sentences from membership in Γ*. Combined with the closure properties of Γ*, this valuation will be used in the Truth Lemma to show agreement between semantic satisfaction and syntactic membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth Lemma (Lemma 44B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Γ* a complete consistent set and v(Γ*) as defined, v(Γ*) ⊨ α iff α ∈ Γ*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction on formula structure: base case for atoms by definition of v(Γ*); inductive steps use the closure properties of Γ* (e.g., for ¬ and → use equivalences from Proposition 42B). This lemma is the linchpin for proving completeness (a valuation satisfying Γ* satisfies Γ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness Theorem (Theorem 45A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is consistent, then Γ is satisfiable (i.e., has a model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: extend Γ to a complete consistent Γ* (Lindenbaum); define valuation v(Γ*); apply Truth Lemma to conclude v(Γ*) satisfies every α ∈ Γ*, hence every α ∈ Γ. This is the syntactic ↔ semantic completeness in the form 'consistent implies satisfiable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of entailment and derivability (Corollary 45B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For all Γ and sentences α: if Γ ⊨ α then Γ ⊢ α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by contraposition: if Γ ⊬ α then Γ ∪ {¬α} is consistent, hence satisfiable (by completeness), contradicting Γ ⊨ α. Thus semantic entailment implies syntactic derivability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of finitely satisfiable (Definition 46A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set Γ of wffs is finitely satisfiable iff every finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ is satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finitely satisfiable captures the idea that no finite subset produces a contradiction; it is the hypothesis in the Compactness Theorem that yields global satisfiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness Theorem (Theorem 46B)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Γ ⊨ α iff there is a finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ such that Γ0 ⊨ α. 2) Γ is satisfiable iff it is finitely satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses soundness and completeness: (2) if every finite subset of Γ is satisfiable then every finite subset is consistent, so Γ is consistent (Proposition 33H), and by completeness Γ is satisfiable. (1) follows from (2) via entailment ↔ inconsistency of Γ ∪ {¬α}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct compactness proof via finitely satisfiable extension (Lemma 47B & Theorem 47C)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finitely satisfiable set Γ can be extended to a complete and finitely satisfiable Γ*; then constructing v(Γ*) and applying a version of the Truth Lemma yields satisfiability of Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction is parallel to Lindenbaum's but ensures at each step that one of Γn∪{αn} or Γn∪{¬αn} remains finitely satisfiable. The key technical step is showing finite-satisfiability is preserved at each extension stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive formation of wffs (Definition 52A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Atomic wffs (e.g., P a, P vi) are wffs; if α is a wff then ¬α is a wff; if α and β are wffs then (α ∧ β) is a wff; if α is a wff then ∃vi α is a wff, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wffs are defined inductively so structural induction can be applied. This unique/readable formation ensures that syntactic and semantic definitions (and inductive proofs about them) are well-founded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of structures and satisfaction for wffs with variables
rubrics_metrics.description: A structure A provides a domain |A|, interpretations of constants (a^A ∈ |A|) and predicates (P^A ⊆ |A|). Satisfaction is defined relative to A and a variable assignment s: |=_A P a [s] iff a^A ∈ P^A; |=_A P vi [s] iff s(vi) ∈ P^A; |=_A ¬α [s] iff not |=_A α [s]; |=_A (α ∧ β) [s] iff |=_A α [s] and |=_A β [s]; |=_A ∃vi α [s] iff |=_A α [s[m/vi]] for some m ∈ |A|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variable assignments s are functions mapping every variable to an element of |A|. s[m/vi] denotes the assignment equal to s except mapping vi to m. This machinery is needed to give precise semantics to quantifiers and formulas with variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sentence and free/bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence is a wff with no free occurrences of variables. Free/bound occurrences are defined inductively: atomic occurrences are free; in ¬β an occurrence is free iff it is free in β; in (β ∧ γ) an occurrence is free iff free in β or γ; in ∃x β, occurrences of x in β become bound (no occurrence of x in ∃x β is free).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since satisfaction of wffs depends on variable assignments only through free variables, sentences are precisely those wffs whose satisfaction is independent of assignments; thus one can write |=_A α (no [s]) for sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution and the ∀-elimination (instantiation) rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution α(t/x) replaces free occurrences of x in α by term t; one often wants the rule: from ∀x α infer α(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitution must be defined carefully (inductively) to avoid variable capture; not every term can be substituted for every variable in every formula. Semantic justification: |=_A α(t) [s] iff |=_A α [s[m/x]] where m is the element denoted by t in A. Formal inference rules depend on a precise substitution definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model and theory notions; axiomatization example
rubrics_metrics.description: A structure A is a model of a set Γ of sentences iff A satisfies all sentences in Γ. Example: the two sentences ∀v0 P v0v0 and ∀v0 ∀v1 ∀v2 ((P v0v1 ∧ P v1v2) → P v0v2) axiomatize preorders (reflexive, transitive relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can study which classes of structures are axiomatizable by sets of sentences and what properties are expressible. Compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem impose limits (e.g., finiteness of the domain is not expressible in first-order logic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness and completeness of derivation systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Soundness: if Γ ⊢ α then Γ ⊨ α. Completeness: if Γ ⊨ α then Γ ⊢ α. Equivalently, 'consistent iff satisfiable' is a form of completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soundness is usually proved by induction on derivations. Completeness is harder and is proved via Lindenbaum's Lemma, construction of Γ*, definition of v(Γ*), and the Truth Lemma. Consequences include the Compactness Theorem and Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem; further, completeness ensures every consistent theory has a model.
